name: The Bible
fw: CCSS RL/RI/RH / C3 / IL SS 9–12 / Teaching About Religion
fwnote: The course reads a tradition's texts as literature and as historical sources in a public school, so it cites the reading standards for the band (RL, RI, RH, WHST), C3 history for 6–8, Illinois SS.H 9–12, and one of the six principles in "A Teacher's Guide to Religion in the Public Schools" (First Amendment Center) that the AAR 2010 Guidelines build on; alignment is the course author's judgment, not a certification or an endorsement by any of these bodies.

1.bq: What do the first stories in Genesis say about the beginning of the world?
std: RL.K.2
With prompting and support, retell familiar stories with their key details.
Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Describe the characters, settings and major events of a story using key details.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
1.write: Pick one story: the seven days, the garden, or Noah. Tell it in order. Say what happens first, next and last. Say "the story says." Name the book it comes from: Genesis.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: Seven Days and a Garden
ch.bq: What does the first story in the Bible say about how the world began?
ch.talk: What is the first thing you would want to hear about in a story about the beginning of the world?
ch.story: The Biggest Book in the House

l.look: Which part has more books, the Old Testament or the New Testament?
What is one thing the two families do the same? What is one thing they do differently?
In the story, what happens right after God speaks?
Which day comes first: fish and birds, or sun and moon?
Why do you think a story would put one rule in a place with so much to enjoy?
How do you think Adam and Eve felt as they walked out of the garden?

ch.t: Noah and the Rainbow
ch.bq: What does the story of Noah say about a big flood and a promise?
ch.talk: What is a promise someone made to you? How did you know they would keep it?

l.look: Which is the biggest number? Is the boat longer or taller?
What two animals would you want to see first in the line? What sounds would you hear?
Why did a leaf tell Noah the water was going down?
What is something you use to help you remember a promise?
What do you do when someone talks in words you do not understand?
Name one thing the two stories share and one thing that is only in Genesis.

2.bq: What holds a family together in the stories of Genesis?
std: Describe the characters, settings and major events of a story using key details.
Retell stories, fables and folktales from different cultures and state the lesson or message they teach.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
2.write: Pick one person from this unit: Abraham, Sarah, Rebekah, Jacob, Esau or Joseph. Tell one thing the story says they did. Say which part of Genesis it is in. Then tell what you think about it.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: Abraham, Sarah and a Promise
ch.bq: What does the story say a promise can do for a family?
ch.talk: Have you ever tried to count the stars? What did it feel like?
ch.story: More Stars Than You Can Count

l.look: What would you pack if you had to walk to a new home?
Why do you think the story picks stars, and not rocks or trees?
How is the first laugh different from the second laugh?
Ten camels drink a lot. What does that tell you about Rebekah?
Jacob was scared. What did Esau do instead of being mean?
Why do you think the angels go both up and down?
Which row has the biggest number? Whose family is that?

ch.t: Joseph and His Brothers
ch.bq: What does the story say happens when someone chooses to forgive?
ch.talk: How do you think the brothers felt when they saw the coat?

l.look: If you were one of the eleven, what would you want to say to your father?
Joseph had eleven brothers. What do the eleven stars stand for?
Did Reuben and Judah do enough to help Joseph? What else could they have done?
Why would thin cows eating fat cows be a scary dream for a king?
Why was it smart to save grain in the good years?

l.t: The Brothers Come to Buy Food
l.look: Why do you think Joseph did not tell them who he was right away?
Joseph says the bad thing turned into a good thing. What good thing?

3.bq: How does the Exodus story say a people went from slaves to free?
std: Describe the characters, settings and major events of a story using key details.
Ask and answer who, what, where, when, why and how questions about a story's key details.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
3.write: Was Moses brave? Tell about two parts of the story. Use the basket story in Exodus 2, the bush in Exodus 3, or the sea in Exodus 14. Say what the story says. Then say what you think.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: A Baby in a Basket
ch.bq: How does the story say a baby in a basket grew up to be a leader?
ch.talk: The big sister stayed to watch the basket. Why do you think she stayed?

l.look: How did one family turn into a whole people? Tell it in your own words.
Why was the new king afraid of the Israelites?
Why did the mother paint the basket with tar? What would happen without it?
The princess knew the baby was an Israelite. She kept him anyway. What does that tell you about her?
How was Moses's life in Midian different from his life in Egypt?
What did Moses see that was strange? What did he say when God called his name?
Who is the message from, and who carried it? Say it in your own words.

ch.t: Through the Sea to a Mountain
ch.bq: How does the story say the people got out of Egypt and what did they get at the mountain?
ch.talk: What would you see, hear and feel walking between two walls of water?

l.look: Which plague came first? Which came last on this list?
Why did the people eat with their shoes on and their sticks in their hands?
Draw or describe what the people saw on their right and on their left.
The people called this food manna. Why do you think they gave it that name?
Pick one rule. Tell what it looks like to keep it at school.
How many days of work come before the day of rest?
Why do you think families tell the same story every year?

4.bq: What do these stories say about being brave and being kind?
std: Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Retell stories, fables and folktales from different cultures and state the lesson or message they teach.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
4.write: Pick one brave person from this unit: David, Daniel, Jonah or the Samaritan. Tell what the story says he did. Name the book the story is in, like 1 Samuel 17 or Luke 10. Then say why you think it was brave or kind.
rooms: Daily Practice — The Bible, grades K–2

ch.t: David, Daniel and Jonah
ch.bq: What does it look like to be brave in these old stories?
ch.talk: David was small and the giant was big. Why do you think David was not afraid?

l.look: What do you think the shepherd boy will do next? What makes a good shepherd?
Goliath had a sword. What did David say he had? What do you think that means?
Which part of David's life would you pick to draw? Why that part?
Which number is the biggest? Which psalm is the shortest?
The psalm calls God a shepherd. What does a shepherd do that the psalm talks about?
Daniel knew the rule and prayed anyway. Was that brave, or something else? What do you think?
What do you think Jonah was thinking inside the fish? What would you do first when you got out?
Which two numbers are the same? Which story does each number come from?

ch.t: Stories Jesus Told
ch.bq: Why did Jesus teach with stories, and what do Christians remember about him?
ch.talk: Two people walked past. One stopped. Why do you think Jesus made the helper someone nobody expected?

l.look: How many Gospels are there? Which number is the biggest?
The angel says "David's town." Which town is that? Who else in this unit came from there?
What is the same in both stories? What is different? Why might two writers tell it differently?
The shepherd is happiest about one sheep, not ninety-nine. What do you think the story is trying to say?
Who was a neighbor in this picture? How is it like the story Jesus told?
What is something small you have seen grow big? Why might Jesus tell a story about a seed?
The disciples said no. Jesus said yes. Why do you think this story is a favorite for kids?
Which story from this chapter goes with Christmas? Which Bible part tells both of these stories?

5.bq: What is the Bible, and how does its first big story hold together?
std: Use text features and search tools, such as key words and labels, to locate information quickly.
Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
5.write: Is the Torah more a book of stories or a book of rules? Cite two or three passages from this unit (for example Genesis 12:2, Exodus 20:8–12 and Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Say what each passage says, and explain how a Jewish reader and a Christian reader might each use it.

ch.t: A Library of Books
ch.bq: Why do people call the Bible one book when it is really a whole library?
ch.talk: The four books had the same first line but different lists of books. What do you think could make a book list change from one group to another?

l.look: How would you read that big book differently than you would read a single story? Which part would you look for first?
Why does the same set of books get a different name from each reader? Which name would you use in a school report, and why?
The Hebrew Bible and the Protestant Old Testament hold the same text. How can one be 24 books and the other 39?
Psalms has 150 chapters, but each one is a song. Why might a book of songs need so many numbered parts?
Christians treasure this verse. Find the three parts of its address: book, chapter and verse. Which part tells you it is in the New Testament?
Which card is a law, which a song, which a letter, and which a story? What clue on each card told you?
Why might the New Testament writers choose Greek instead of Hebrew for their letters and Gospels?
A Christian translation from 1611 and a Jewish translation from 1917 begin with the same sentence. What does that tell you about how carefully translators work?
The three translations use different words for the same Greek sentence. Does the meaning change? Which one would be easiest for a new reader?
Ezra's helpers explained the reading so people understood. How is that like what happens in a synagogue, a church or a classroom today?
What rules would you want at that table so that every person could speak and be heard? How could those rules help our class?

ch.t: The Torah's Big Story: Creation to Sinai
ch.bq: How do five books tell one long story from the making of the world to the edge of a promised land?
ch.talk: The map goes from Ur to Egypt to the edge of Canaan but never into it. Why do you think the Torah ends right at the edge, before the people go in?

l.look: Genesis is the longest of the five. It covers creation, the flood and four generations of one family. Why might a book that covers so much need the most chapters?
Which student's idea fits better with a book that has stories, songs and speeches as well as rules? Explain your answer.
In this verse, how does the story say God makes light? What does this tell you about the way Genesis 1 pictures creation?
The word bow here means rainbow, and token means sign. Who is the covenant between? Why might a rainbow be a good sign for a promise about rain?
Thee and thy mean you and your. What three things does the text say God promises Abraham here? Which promise would take the longest to come true?
What choices does Joseph have at this moment? Genesis says he forgives them in the end. Why might the story make forgiving so hard and slow?
Moses asks what name to give the people. What answer does the text give? Why do you think this answer has puzzled and interested readers for so long?
The numbers 40, 12 and 10 come up again and again in these books. Why might a story use the same numbers over and over?
One of these two commandments is about time and one is about family. Which one gives a reason for keeping it? What is the reason?

s.t: The Long Road and the Covenant

l.look: Why do you think the crowd believed the ten and not the two? What does the story seem to say about fear and trust?
Jews say these words morning and evening. Christians know them because the Gospels say Jesus quoted them. What does the verse ask a person to do, and with how much of themselves?

6.t: The Land, the Judges and the Kings
6.bq: What do the stories of the judges and the first kings show about what their readers valued in a leader?
std: Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Work out a story's theme from its details and summarize the text.
Determine a theme from how characters respond to challenges, and summarize the text.
Teaching About Religion · inform not conform
Inform students about beliefs without asking them to conform to any.
6.write: What did these books say a good leader was? Choose two or three passages from the unit, such as Joshua 1:9, Judges 21:25, Ruth 1:16, 1 Samuel 16:7 or 1 Kings 3:9. Say what each passage says about a leader. Then explain how Jewish readers, Christian readers or scholars have read it. Use your own words.

ch.t: Joshua, Judges and Ruth
ch.bq: What do the stories of Joshua, Judges and Ruth show about what a people valued?
ch.talk: Ruth chooses to stay with Naomi when she could have gone home. What do you think made her choose that?
ch.story: Where You Go, I Will Go

l.look: This verse uses old words like thee and whithersoever. Say it again in your own words. Who is speaking, and to whom?
The story uses the number seven again and again. Where else in the Bible have you seen the number seven? Why might a storyteller repeat it?
Ruth is the shortest book here. Why might a very short book still be one of the most read?
Why set up a stone? What does a stone do that a spoken promise cannot?
Why might a writer tell the same pattern over and over instead of once? What does the reader learn from the repeating?
Why might the Bible keep both a prose version and a song version of the same event? What can a song do that a report cannot?
The numbers go down each time. What does the text say is the reason for sending men home? What is the storyteller trying to show?
This is the last line of the book. Is it a complaint, a description or a hint about what comes next? Say which you think and why.
Count the promises Ruth makes in this one sentence. Which one do you think was hardest to keep?

l.t: A Field, a Wedding and a King
l.look: Think about what a people chooses to keep and retell. What does keeping the book of Ruth tell you about what its readers valued?

ch.t: Samuel, Saul, David and Solomon
ch.bq: What did the books of Samuel and Kings say a king was supposed to be, and how did the first kings measure up?
ch.talk: Solomon never meant to use the sword. What did he really want to find out, and why did his plan work?
ch.story: One Baby, Two Mothers and a Sword

l.look: If you cut one long book into two, where would you cut it? Look at how 1 Samuel ends and 2 Samuel begins, and say whether that was a good place.
The elders give two reasons for wanting a king. What are they? Which reason do you think mattered more to them?
Is Saul's story a sad story or a warning story? Point to one thing in the text that supports your answer.
Countenance means face. Stature means height. Put this verse in your own words. Why does the story include it before David appears?
Why might a copyist make a giant taller over time, or shorter? Does the size change what the story means?
David could have ended his years of hiding in one moment. What does the story want readers to see about him by showing what he did not do?
Both David and Solomon are given forty years. Forty is also the number of days of rain in Noah's story and years in the wilderness. What might the number mean in the Bible?
Nathan waits until David has judged the rich man before he says this. Why did he not just tell David what he had done wrong?
Solomon could have asked for anything. What does his choice tell you about what the book thinks a king is for?
A cubit is about 18 inches. Work out the length of the Temple in feet. Is it bigger or smaller than your school gym?
Put each piece of advice in your own words. What does the writer want readers to think about a king who takes the second kind?

7.bq: How did a people keep their story alive through warning, loss and going home?
std: Explain how poems, drama and prose differ, using their structural elements.
Work out a story's theme from its details and summarize the text.
Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
7.write: Pick this question: What did the prophets say would happen, and what gave the people hope after it did? Use two or three passages from this unit, such as Amos 5:24, 2 Kings 25, Psalm 137:1 or Ezekiel 37:1–14. For each one, say what the text says. Then tell how Jewish or Christian readers have read it.

ch.t: Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the Exile
ch.bq: Why did the prophets say hard things, and what happened when nobody listened?
ch.talk: Jeremiah kept speaking even when people laughed at him. Why do you think he did not stop?

l.look: Which student is closer to what the Bible means by a prophet? What in Jeremiah's message tells you?

l.t: Elijah and the Fire on Carmel
l.look: Elijah's prayer is short. What does he ask the people to learn from what happens next?
The story lists three loud things and then one quiet thing. Why do you think the writer put them in that order?
Amos compares fairness to a river. A river keeps moving and never stops. What does that picture say about how fairness should work?
Isaiah names two groups of people to protect. Why do you think he picked those two?
What is the one idea both lines share? Try writing your own two lines that say one idea two ways.
Years BCE count down. How many years passed between the fall of Samaria and the fall of Jerusalem?
The king thought burning the scroll would end the message. Did it? What does the story say happened next?
The writer lists what was burned and who was taken. Why do you think the writer gives these facts without adding feelings?
The singer says "we" and not "I." What does that tell you about who this song was for?
Ezekiel does not answer yes or no. Why might the writer have him answer that way?

ch.t: Psalms, Proverbs, Daniel, Esther and Home Again
ch.bq: How did songs, wise sayings and brave stories help a people keep going, and what did going home look like?
ch.talk: Esther had to choose between staying safe and speaking up. What made her decide to speak?

l.look: Here "want" means to be in need. What does a shepherd give sheep that they would otherwise lack?
This is the last verse of the whole book of Psalms. Why is it a good line to end on?
Which of the five books has the most psalms? Count them from the numbers.
Wrath means anger. Grievous means harsh. Tell about a time when a soft answer calmed someone down.
Eliphaz thinks bad things only happen to bad people. What does Job's own story say about that idea?
Daniel could have prayed in secret. Why do you think the story has him keep the window open?
Mordecai asks a question instead of giving an order. Why might a question work better here?
About how many years were the people in exile before Cyrus let them go home?
The text says helpers explained the words. Why was explaining as important as reading?
Why do you think the writer took the time to name so many builders? What does the list say about how the wall got done?

8.bq: How does the New Testament tell the story of Jesus and his first followers, and how have its readers understood that story?
std: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view shapes the way events are told.
Compare stories in the same genre for how they approach similar themes and topics.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
8.write: Pick a question: How does Luke show who counts as a neighbor? Or: What did a letter do for a church far from Paul? Use two or three passages from this unit (such as Luke 10:25–37, Luke 15:11–32, Acts 2:1–4, 1 Corinthians 13:1–13). Tell what each passage says and how Christians and other readers have understood it.

ch.t: The Life of Jesus in the Gospels
ch.bq: How do four different books tell the story of one life, and why do Christians read all four?
ch.talk: The father ran before the son said one word. What do you think the story wants its listeners to notice about the father?

l.look: Which Gospel is the shortest? Which two are closest in length?
What might it feel like to hold that coin? Why might people hope for a leader sent by God?
Why might Luke choose shepherds, ordinary workers, to be the first visitors?
What is the same in both churches? What is different? Why might each church do it its way?
The men caught fish for a living. What might "fishers of men" mean in their new job?
Which parables appear only in Luke? What does that tell you about Luke's Gospel?

l.t: A Neighbor and a Lost Son
l.look: The lawyer asked "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus asked a different question back. How is it different?
What is a peacemaker? Name one thing a peacemaker at school might do.
What does the story say about the four friends? Why might Mark include them and not just the man on the mat?
How are the two practices alike? How are they different? What does each one remember?

l.t: The Cross and the Empty Tomb
l.look: Who are the first people to hear this news in Matthew? Why might that matter to readers?

ch.t: Acts, Paul's Letters and the Early Church
ch.bq: How did a small group of followers in Jerusalem grow into churches around the sea, and what did they write to each other?
ch.talk: Why might a letter matter so much to a group that met in one house? What can a letter do that a visit cannot?

l.look: Put the four places in order from closest to farthest. How does that order match the way the book of Acts unfolds?
Why might Luke list so many places? What is the story saying about who the message is for?
What would be hard about living this way? What would be good about it?
Pick one word for Saul before and one word for Saul after. What changed, and what stayed the same?
Find each city on a map of the Mediterranean. Which way did Paul move over time, east or west?
Restate each side in your own words. What did the meeting decide, and what did it still ask of Gentiles?
Which letter is the longest? Philemon is one chapter; who do you think it was written to, a big church or one person?
"Abideth" means "stays." Charity here means love. Why might Paul put love above faith and hope?
Which of the three is hardest for you? Why might a letter to a whole church say this?
Why might a church in a hard time want to hear this passage read aloud?
Add up the rows. Which kind of book makes up most of the New Testament?

9.t: Genres and How to Read Them
9.bq: How does knowing what kind of writing a passage is change the questions a careful reader asks?
std: Describe how a text presents information, such as in order, by comparison or by cause.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text, including terms specific to history and society.
Work out figurative and connotative meanings and the effect of repetition and sound in poetry.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
9.write: Pick two passages from this unit that belong to different genres, such as Exodus 21:28–30 and Psalm 19:1, or Amos 5:24 and 1 Thessalonians 1:1. Explain what kind of writing each one is and name two clues that show it. Then tell how the genre changes what a reader asks of the passage, and give one example of how a Jewish, Christian or academic reader has read it.
rooms: How to read a sacred text — the room

ch.t: Law, Narrative and Genealogy
ch.bq: How does knowing what kind of writing a passage is change the way we read it?
ch.talk: Think of a recipe and a poem about the same meal. What would you look for in each one that you would not look for in the other?

l.look: Which piece is a report, which is a law and which is a poem? Name one clue in each that told you.
Genesis is the longest and is almost all story. Leviticus is the shortest and is almost all law. What might that tell you about how much space each genre takes?

l.t: Studying a Sacred Text at School
l.look: Which sentence describes without asserting or denying a belief? What is the difference between describing a belief and holding one?
What does the passage tell you, and what does it leave out? List one gap a reader would want filled.
This is the only verdict the narrator gives in the whole chapter. Why might a storyteller wait until the last verse to say it?
The phrase repeats and then changes. What does the change from 'good' to 'very good' tell a listener about how the chapter is built?
These commands have no 'if' and no stated penalty. What kind of law are they, and what would a case law about stealing have to add?
Two versions, two reasons for the same rest day. What does each reason ask a reader to remember?
Both codes agree that a warned owner is responsible. Where do they differ, and what might each difference say about what the community valued?
Enoch's number breaks the pattern, and the text says of him only that he walked with God and was not. Why might a list built on repetition include one line that is different?

l.t: Who, for Whom, When and Why
l.look: Ask the four questions of this one verse: who might have written it, for whom, when and why? Which answers come from tradition and which from scholars?

ch.t: Poetry, Prophecy, Gospel, Letter, Apocalypse
ch.bq: What clues tell a reader that a passage is a poem, a prophecy, a gospel, a letter or an apocalypse, and what does each one ask of us?
ch.talk: Which card would you have found hardest to name, and what clue would you look for next time?

l.t: Say It, Then Say It Again
l.look: Match each word in the first line to its partner in the second. What does the second line make more concrete?
List what you know about a well-watered tree and about chaff. Which of those facts does the psalm want you to apply to a person?
The Hebrew alphabet has 22 letters. Which numbers here are multiples of 22, and what does the one that is not tell you?
Amos spoke this to people who were cheating the poor. How does the water image work as a demand about the present rather than a prediction?
Why break a jar instead of just saying the words? What can a sign-act do that a speech cannot?
Find the two halves. Which words in the first half are matched by opposites in the second? Describe a situation this saying is about.

l.t: An Ancient Life with a Purpose
l.look: This opening names its subject and states a claim about him in one line. What does it tell you about the writer's purpose before any story begins?
Mark is the shortest and, many scholars think, the earliest. If Matthew and Luke used Mark, what might they have added to make their books longer?
Find the three parts of an ancient greeting: the senders, the receivers and the wish. Who is being written to, and where?
Add the rows. What share of the New Testament's 27 books are letters? Why might letters have been so useful to a movement spread across many cities?
Later in the chapter an angel says the four beasts are four kingdoms. Why might a writer under a hostile empire choose to show kingdoms as beasts rather than name them?
Seven and twelve keep returning. What did each number mean in the Hebrew Bible, and what would a first-century reader have understood when they saw it again?

10.t: The Pentateuch as Literature and History
10.bq: How do the five books of the Torah tell a people's story of beginnings, promise and law, and how have different readers understood the same words?
std: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources.
Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.
Determine a theme, analyze how it develops through characters, setting and plot, and summarize objectively.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
10.write: How does the Torah use a story to explain a law? Choose one law and one story, for example Exodus 20:2 and the escape from Egypt, Leviticus 19:34 and Genesis 12, or Deuteronomy 5:15 and Exodus 1. Cite two or three passages by book, chapter and verse. Explain what each says, how the story and the law connect, and how at least two different readers, Jewish, Christian or scholarly, have read them.

ch.t: Genesis: Creation, Flood, Ancestors
ch.bq: How does Genesis tell the story of beginnings, and what do its readers, ancient and modern, make of it?
ch.talk: If two ancient stories share a boat, a flood and birds, what are the different ways a reader might explain that?
ch.story: The Tablet in the Glass Case

l.look: Read the verse aloud. Which words does the writer choose to start the whole Bible with, and why might that matter?
Compare this with Genesis 1:27, where God creates by speaking. What picture of God does each verse give?
Which details in the columns would each reader point to in support of their view? Can both readers be honest about the same text?
The text never answers Cain's question. What do you think the writer wants the reader to do with it?
Which of these numbers seem to overlap or repeat? How might a traditional reader and a source-critical scholar each explain that?
Pick one detail the stories share and one they do not. What does each difference suggest about how the writers thought about God or the gods?
What do the builders say they want? What happens to that wish by the end of verse 9?
Compare this with Genesis 11:4, where the builders want to "make us a name." What is the writer doing by placing the two so close together?
The narrator never says Jacob got what he deserved. How does the writer hint at it anyway? Find the echo between the two scenes.
God never speaks in the Joseph story. How does this line, spoken by Joseph, tell the reader how to understand everything before it?
Genesis 1 to 11 covers all peoples; Genesis 12 to 50 covers one family. Roughly what share of the book is about the ancestors?

ch.t: Exodus to Deuteronomy: Covenant and Law
ch.bq: How do Exodus through Deuteronomy turn a story of escape into a set of laws, and how have readers counted, kept and debated those laws?
ch.talk: Why might a story put a list of laws right after a scene of thunder, smoke and fear? What does the setting do to the list?
ch.story: At the Foot of the Mountain

l.look: What might the writer be saying by naming the midwives and not the king? How does that choice shape who the reader remembers?
The 1917 JPS translation leaves this phrase in Hebrew letters. Why might a translator choose not to translate a name?
Darkness and the death of the firstborn follow as 9 and 10. The plagues move from the river to the sky to the house. Do you see a pattern in the order?
List two things only the story tells and two things only the song does. Why might a writer include both?
